title: The Skull and Crossbones List
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that once students are writing in large quantities, teachers should turn to quality by building a Skull and Crossbones list of basic writing errors that are unacceptable at the secondary level. The list is not pre-populated; it is built from the first pieces of student writing, with no marking on papers, and limited to five or fewer non-recursive problems such as lowercase sentence openers or missing end punctuation. He introduces each item in a notebook mini-lesson with a problem and solution example, then posts the list in the room all year. From then on, any polished piece containing a listed error comes back with a frowny face and is a zero until the student fixes it. He frames this as unemotional accountability from someone who cares, not harshness, and notes that parents rarely object because students can simply revise and resubmit.
points: Quantity of writing comes first, but once it is in place a short, responsive list of habitual errors is the cheapest way to lift quality.
Choose list items that are non-recursive (capitalization, end punctuation) rather than things like comma placement, which get harder as sentences get more complex.
Hold the line without marking up papers: return the work with a frownie face, record a zero until the student fixes it, and let the posted list serve as the reference.
The deeper aim is cultural: teaching students that details matter and that a basic level of care is part of doing hard things well.
quotes: If we're going to improve the quality of writing our students are capable of — an absolutely critical endeavor — then we first need to ensure that our kids have a large amount of writing that they do. Quantity precedes quality.
As I'm identifying these things, I don't mark a single thing on their papers — I'm just populating the Skull and Crossbones list. If I have to put a grade, it's credit / no credit.

For example, placing commas correctly is something that gets harder over time because the kinds of sentences students are trying to create get more complex over time. But capitalizing things doesn't really do that. It's not recursive.
As time progresses, I'll add things as needed. I don't want to create 100 things on this list, but a dozen or two goes a long way.

If a team of athletes wanted to be elite — if they wanted to do hard things — they would certainly be silly to think they'd get there by being sloppy in the most basic elements of their sport. I want all of my students to have the chance now to be held unemotionally accountable for a basic attention to detail by someone who loves them (me). I want them to know that, in truth, details do matter — that it pays to attend to them.
I think this is one reason that parents don't tend to complain about this. The student is free to fix her problems and re-submit.
